name: Basketball
tagline: Peach baskets in a Massachusetts gym became the world's slickest show.
overview: Basketball is played by two teams of five on a rectangular court, scoring by putting a leather ball through a hoop mounted 3.05 meters high at each end. Dribbling, passing, and shooting are the entire grammar, and the hoop sits low enough that every player on the floor, point guard to center, is a threat to score. Nothing between the athletes and the air but a wooden floor and a rulebook.

Invented in 1891 by James Naismith to keep athletes busy through a New England winter, it became the most exported indoor sport on earth — FIBA counts 212 national federations, from superpowers to islands. The NBA turned it into global theater, the WNBA proved a women's professional league could last a quarter century and counting, and one rusted hoop still runs a waiting game in every city in the world.

The newcomer's shortcut is that basketball is won with feet before hands. Learn to stop, pivot, and square up before chasing flashy handles, and the rest of the game opens up. The other shortcut: play. Pickup basketball is the sport's true academy, and it takes all comers.
facts: 1891 — James Naismith posts 13 rules at the YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, with peach baskets as goals
FIBA (world, founded 1932); the NBA (1946) and WNBA (1997) run the premier professional leagues
5 v 5, with unlimited substitutions at stoppages; NBA clubs carry 15 players on standard contracts
Four 12-minute quarters in the NBA, four 10-minute quarters under FIBA rules
28 x 15 m (FIBA) or 94 x 50 ft (NBA); hoop at 3.05 m, three-point arc at 6.75 m FIBA and 7.24 m NBA
Men since 1936, women since 1976; 3x3 added at the Tokyo 2020 Games
212 FIBA member federations — among the largest sporting families on earth
history: Naismith nails up peach baskets in a Springfield gymnasium and writes 13 rules for an indoor winter game.
The game spreads through YMCA networks and colleges; Senda Berenson adapts it for women within months; it debuts as an Olympic sport at Berlin 1936.
The Basketball Association of America forms in 1946 and absorbs the NBL in 1949 to become the NBA.
The rival ABA runs nine seasons and leaves the NBA the three-point line; the 1979 NCAA final between Magic Johnson and Larry Bird ignites the modern boom.
The USA's Dream Team — Jordan, Magic, Bird — takes the Barcelona Olympics and globalizes the NBA product overnight.
The WNBA tips off and becomes the most durable professional women's team league in the world.
3x3 makes its Olympic debut in Tokyo — the half-court street version that now carries its own World Tour.
formats: 5 v 5 (indoor)
The full game: four quarters on the full court — the format of the NBA, FIBA, and the Olympics.
Half-court, one hoop, 10 minutes or first to 21, on a 12-second shot clock — basketball at double speed, Olympic since 2020.
Streetball
Playground basketball with looser rules and a heavy accent on one-on-one moves; Harlem's Rucker League is its cathedral.
Wheelchair basketball
A Paralympic fixture since Rome 1960 — 5 v 5 with dribbling adapted to chair pushes, played at startling skill.
Half-court 21
The pickup standard: make-it-take-it scoring by ones and twos to 21 — where most players actually live.
skills: Shooting form
Set feet, elbow in, one smooth line from legs to follow-through; the jumper is built from the floor up.
Form shooting one-handed from 1 m, 50 makes, stepping back a meter at a time; track makes per day, not attempts.
Dribbling
Control with the finger pads, eyes up, the ball on a string in both hands.
Five minutes of stationary two-ball drills daily, then full-speed cone series; test: 30 seconds of crossovers without looking down.
Layup
The two-step finish off the correct foot (right hand jumps off the left), plus inside-hand and reverse variants.
Full-speed reps from both wings and the middle — 40 makes per side, finishing through light contact.
Passing
Chest, bounce, and overhead passes delivered to the shooter's pocket, not their body.
Two-player series of 50 per pass type, then the 3-man weave at game speed; count turnovers per 100 passes in scrimmage.
Rebounding
Box out first, jump second — the miss belongs to whoever takes the space.
Partner box-out drill 3 x 30 seconds, then tip drills off the rim; track rebounds per scrimmage quarter.
Pick-and-roll
The two-man game: the screener's defender and the ball-handler's defender forced to guard one action.
Read drills at walking speed — reject, turn the corner, hit the roller — 20 reads each before adding a live defender.
Man defense
Slide-run-slide footwork an arm's length off the ball, sprinting to recover when beaten.
Defensive-slide ladders 3 x 20 seconds, then 1 v 1 to a single hoop; win by forcing a miss within five dribbles.
rules: Five players per side on court, with unlimited substitutions during stoppages.
Score 2 points per field goal, 3 from behind the arc, 1 per free throw — top-level games finish in the 80s to 130s.
You cannot run with the ball: the dribble ends when you gather it, and moving your pivot foot is a travel.
The shot clock resets the attack — 24 seconds in the NBA and FIBA, 14 after an offensive rebound.
Personal fouls: five fouls out under FIBA rules, six in the NBA; team fouls beyond the limit put opponents on the line.
The three-second rule keeps big men from camping in the paint, and goaltending bans touching a shot on its way down.
Zone defense is legal nearly everywhere, though NBA rules add a defensive three-second restriction — know your league's book.
equipment: Ball
Size 7 (about 75 cm) for men 13 and up, size 6 for women's and under-12 play; indoor composite or leather balls run $40-120.
Hoop
A 3.05 m rim on a backboard — portable adjustable systems from $150 let you lower it for learners and raise it as they grow.
Shoes
Court shoes with flat, grippy soles and lateral support; $60-150 buys real protection — running shoes roll ankles on hardwood.
Clothing
Breathable kit plus a mouthguard for organized play; nothing else is mandatory for pickup.
Ball pump
The unglamorous essential — a ball at the wrong pressure teaches a wrong shot.
Cones and a rebounder
A dozen cones and a passing rebounder turn a driveway into a gym for under $60.
training: Build repeat-sprint capacity: the game is a thousand changes of direction over 40 minutes, so shuttle intervals (30 seconds on, 30 off) beat steady jogging.
Jump training with a plan: depth drops to stuck landings first, then box jumps and bounds — the sport pays vertically.
Protect knees and ankles: single-leg RDLs, Copenhagen planks, and barefoot-balance ankle work cut the two most common injuries.
Shoot daily for volume, not variety — 150-300 makes a day of the same footwork patterns beats a new move every week.
Play 1 v 1 and 2 v 2 weekly; half the court doubles the touches and decisions per minute.
pathway: Grassroots
School teams, community leagues, and driveway pickup — where every professional started.
Youth and club (U10-U18)
Club programs and national development frameworks; in the US, AAU circuits own the spring and summer.
College or academy
NCAA and junior-college basketball in the US; club academies and junior professional contracts elsewhere.
Professional
The NBA and WNBA at the summit; the G League, EuroLeague, and top leagues in dozens of countries pay real wages.
National team
FIBA World Cups and the Olympics; 3x3 offers a second international ladder.
events: NBA Finals
Best-of-seven each June between conference champions — the sport's biggest stage.
FIBA Basketball World Cup
Every four years since 1950; 32 teams since 2023 and the main Olympic qualifier.
Olympic basketball
Every four years — men since 1936, women since 1976, 3x3 since 2020.
WNBA Finals
Best-of-five each October — the championship of the world's longest-running women's pro league.
EuroLeague Final Four
Continental Europe's club crown each May, played at opera-house volume.
legends: Michael Jordan
Chicago Bulls — six championships, six Finals MVPs, five league MVPs; the yardstick every greatest-ever argument is measured against.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
Six titles, a record six MVPs, and the unstoppable skyhook; his 38,387 points stood as the NBA record for 39 years.
LeBron James
Four championships with three franchises and the NBA's all-time scoring record since 2023; two decades of elite play and counting.
Diana Taurasi
The WNBA's all-time leading scorer and a six-time Olympic champion — the most decorated Olympian in basketball history.
Stephen Curry
Two MVPs and four titles built on three-point shooting so prolific it moved where every level of the game shoots from.
getting_started: Get a size-appropriate ball and find a hoop — adjustable or full height — and shoot 20 minutes daily for two weeks.
Learn to dribble without watching the ball: five minutes of stationary two-ball work every session.
Find a local pickup run or beginners' league within a month; game reps are irreplaceable.
Master three shots first — the layup, the free throw, and the set jumper. Everything else is decoration.
Watch one NBA or WNBA game a week tracking a single off-ball player; movement and defense teach fastest.
Add two leg days a week — split squats, calf raises, jump rope — before buying any gear beyond shoes.
glossary: Swish
A made shot that touches nothing but net — the game's cleanest sound.
Crossover
A dribble snapped from one hand to the other to shift a defender; Allen Iverson's version is the genre-defining artwork.
Alley-oop
A pass lobbed at the rim for a teammate to catch and dunk in one motion.
Triple-double
Double figures in three of the five main stats — points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks — in one game.
And-one
A made basket plus a foul: one free throw tacked on as punishment for the defense.
Buzzer-beater
A shot released before the horn that wins or ties as time expires.
In the paint
The colored key around the basket where most of the game's bruises happen.
Fast break
A sprint to score before the defense can set — numbers in your favor, seconds on the clock.
Sixth man
The first substitute off the bench, often closer to a starter in scoring than not.
Euro step
A lateral two-step around a defender in the lane — Ginobili made it famous, and every guard now owns it.

name: Cricket
tagline: A 22-yard duel of bat and ball — for an afternoon or five days.
overview: Cricket pits a batting team against a fielding team around a 22-yard pitch: the batters score runs by hitting the ball and running between the wickets, while the bowlers try to dismiss them — bowled, caught, leg before wicket, a dozen ways. An innings ends when ten wickets fall or the allotted overs run out, and the higher total wins. Everything else is format: five days of Test cat-and-mouse, one day of World Cup chess, three hours of T20 fireworks.

It is the beating heart of a belt of countries from London to Lahore — India treats a series like a second monsoon season, the Ashes has run between England and Australia since 1882, and India-Pakistan matches draw audiences counted in the hundreds of millions. Cricket is also the only major sport whose top-class formats differ in length by a factor of fifty: a Test averages 90 overs a day, a T20 innings is twenty.

Newcomers should know the game is decided at two moments: the bowler's release and the batter's contact. Watch wrists and feet, not the scoreboard. And be patient with the format puzzle — start with T20 (three hours), graduate to one-dayers, and let Test cricket seduce you slowly. It will.
facts: 1744 — the first Laws of Cricket; the Marylebone Cricket Club (founded 1787) has guarded them ever since
International Cricket Council — founded 1909 as the Imperial Cricket Conference; 12 Full Members and more than 90 Associate nations
11 a side, with a 12th man as substitute fielder in first-class cricket
Tests: five days at 90 overs a day. ODIs: 50 overs a side. T20s: 20 overs a side, about three hours
An oval field with boundaries typically 65-90 m across; the pitch is 20.12 m (22 yards) of rolled turf with wickets 71 cm high at each end
Cork wrapped in string and leather: 156-163 g for men's play; one new ball per innings in Tests, another after 80 overs
Played at Paris 1900 (Britain beat France); T20 cricket returns to the Games at Los Angeles 2028
Roughly 2.5 billion fans, concentrated in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Australia, England, South Africa, and the Caribbean
history: 16th-17th c.
Villagers and schoolboys in south-east England play 'creckett'; a 1598 court case records the game at Guildford.
The first Laws of Cricket are published — the pitch is set at 22 yards, where it remains to this day.
The Marylebone Cricket Club forms at Lord's and adopts the Laws — cricket's legislature ever since.
Australia beats England in the first Test at the MCG by 45 runs; England's first home defeat in 1882 births The Ashes.
A rain-ruined Test in Melbourne becomes the first one-day international (1971); the men's World Cup follows in 1975 — two years after the women staged theirs.
The ECB invents Twenty20 in 2003; India's T20 World Cup win in 2007 lights the fuse for the Indian Premier League, launched in 2008.
The World Test Championship crowns its first champion (New Zealand, 2021) and T20 wins an Olympic slot for Los Angeles 2028.
formats: Test cricket
The five-day original: two innings a side, red ball, whites — the format the World Test Championship final now crowns every two years.
One Day International
50 overs a side in colored kit; the World Cup format since 1975 — cricket's middle distance.
20 overs a side in about three hours; the format that rewrote shots, salaries, and the sport's audience.
The Hundred
England's 100-ball-per-side invention (2021), built for television pacing and family nights out.
Club and village cricket
Saturday leagues, declaration cricket, and the tea interval — the sport's social fabric from English villages to Indian maidans.
skills: Cover drive
The classical front-foot stroke through the off side: head over the ball, elbow high, the bat swinging through the line.
Drop feeds in the nets — 40 drives through a target zone between extra cover and mid-off, then throwdowns at increasing pace.
Yorker
A fast, full delivery landing at the base of the stumps — too full to drive, too late to dig out.
Target bowling: place a shoe at the popping crease and bowl six-ball sets aiming to clip it four times in six.
Googly
The leg-spinner's wrong 'un: the wrist turns the ball the other way, deceiving the batter on length and spin.
Bowl it in isolation 20 minutes a session and film from behind the stumps — the goal is an action identical to the stock leg-break.
Bouncer
A short-pitched ball rising at chest or head, cramping the pull shot and planting doubt.
Bowl short at a marked target zone on the pitch: two bouncers per six-ball over — one at the body, one as a surprise.
Sweep
A cross-batted shot played kneeling into a spinning ball, robbing the spinner of turn and length.
Progress from tennis-ball sweeps against a bowling machine at 60 kph to soft-ball spinners — 50 reps building to full pace.
Outswing bowling
Seam upright, wrist behind the ball, one side shined — the ball curves late in the air away from the bat.
Bowl at a single stump with a new ball in 6-ball sets, checking seam presentation every delivery; target four of six landing on the seam.
Wicketkeeping
The crouched, gloved collector standing up to the stumps — footwork first, hands second.
100 collects each side at walking pace, then 20 minutes standing up to spinners; never take your eyes off the ball's last meter.
rules: Each team bats until ten wickets fall or the overs run out — once in limited-overs cricket, twice each in Tests.
An over is six legal deliveries; bowlers change ends every over and may not bowl two overs in succession.
The pitch is 20.12 m (22 yards) long; the stumps at each end stand 71.1 cm high and 22.86 cm apart.
Ten dismissal modes exist, from bowled, caught, and LBW to stumped, hit wicket, and obstructing the field — the LBW law alone runs to a page of conditions.
Limited-overs fields are restricted: only a set number of fielders may stand outside the 30-yard circle in each powerplay phase; Tests have no such limit.
Teams may review umpires' calls through the DRS — usually two unsuccessful reviews per innings, checked by ball-tracking and edge-detection technology.
A tie in limited-overs cricket is broken by a Super Over: one extra over each, the closest thing in sport to extra innings.
equipment: Bat
A willow blade with a cane handle, no more than 96.5 cm long or 10.8 cm wide; $60-150 for a good starter bat, $400+ for pro-grade English willow.
Ball
Cork, string, and stitched leather, 156-163 g for men's play — one quality ball per innings, cheaper composite balls for training.
Pads and gloves
Batting pads, batting gloves, and a keeper's set — the kit that makes the sport survivable; $60-150 entry tier.
Helmet
A grille-faced helmet, mandatory almost everywhere since the 2014-15 safety reforms.
Abdominal guard
The 'box' — non-negotiable for anyone standing up to fast bowling; about $10.
Stumps and bails
Three stumps and two bails per end; a set with a composite ball costs under $40 for garden cricket.
Shoes
Rubber-soled for juniors and artificial pitches, half-spikes or full spikes for bowlers on turf.
training: Net batting with intent: 30-45 minutes of scenario batting (leave the first 20 balls wide of off stump, then score) beats aimless hitting.
Bowlers build work capacity like pitchers — tempo runs, heavy posterior-chain lifting (RDLs, Nordic curls), and strict over counts to manage bone-stress risk.
Fielding is trained as a reaction skill: 20 minutes of catching progressions — high balls, slip catching, flat throws at a single stump — every session.
Rotational power for batting comes from the hips, not the arms: med-ball throws and cable woodchops twice a week.
Play formats deliberately — T20 for shot-making under pressure, longer formats for technique — because each teaches the other.
pathway: Grassroots
Backyard, street, and school cricket — plus soft-ball and tape-ball formats where turf and a leather ball are luxuries.
Junior club (U8-U18)
Weekend age-group and school competitions; hard-ball entry from around under-11s in most countries.
Age representative
District, state, and regional honors feeding national under-19 programs — the Under-19 World Cup is heavily scouted.
First-class and franchise
Premier club leagues into state and first-class contracts; T20 franchises worldwide now offer a parallel career.
International
Central contracts with national boards; the ultimate prizes remain the Ashes urn and a World Cup of any length.
events: ICC Cricket World Cup
Men's 50-over championship every four years since 1975; the women's edition has run since 1973 — two years longer.
T20 World Cup
Held every couple of years since 2007, now with 20 teams — the sport's biggest television property after a World Cup final.
World Test Championship
A two-year league of Test series culminating in a one-off final, first won by New Zealand in 2021.
The Ashes
England v Australia, Test cricket's oldest grudge since 1882 — a series every couple of years, fought over a terracotta urn.
Indian Premier League
March to May every year since 2008: ten franchises, the world's richest cricket league, and a player auction like no other.
WBBL and The Hundred
Franchise competitions (Women's Big Bash since 2015, The Hundred since 2021) that made the women's game genuinely full-time.
legends: Don Bradman
Australia — a Test batting average of 99.94 across 52 Tests; statisticians still rank it the most dominant career in any sport.
Sachin Tendulkar
India — 100 international centuries and 34,357 international runs, both records; carried a billion expectations for 24 years.
Muttiah Muralitharan
Sri Lanka — 800 Test wickets, more than any bowler in history, spun from an action all his own.
Mithali Raj
India — 10,868 international runs and the first woman past 10,000; a 23-year career that professionalized the women's game.
getting_started: Start with a tennis ball and one bat — learn to stop the ball dead before you try to hit it far.
Bowl at a single target on a wall or pitch 20 minutes a day; accuracy arrives years before speed.
Watch one T20 match with a single bowler in focus for a full spell — count where each ball lands.
Join a weekend club or a tape-ball group within a month; cricket is unplayable alone.
Buy the protective basics in order: box, pads, gloves, helmet — then upgrade the bat last.
Play backyard rules (one bounce one hand, six-and-out) to build hitting instinct without a full field.
glossary: Over
Six legal deliveries bowled by one bowler — the game's basic unit of accounting.
Wicket
The three stumps — or a dismissal, or the pitch itself; context is everything.
Maiden
An over conceding no runs — a bowler's shutout.
Duck
Out for zero; a golden duck is first ball.
Googly
The leg-spinner's wrong 'un, turning the opposite way to expectation.
Yorker
A fast, full delivery aimed at the base of the stumps.
Silly point
A fielder standing absurdly close to the batter — helmet mandatory, nerve also required.
Nightwatchman
A tail-end batter sent in late on day one to survive until stumps, protecting a specialist.
DRS
The Decision Review System — teams challenging calls with ball-tracking and edge-detection technology.
Ashes
The England-Australia Test urn, born of a mock obituary mourning English cricket in 1882.

name: Baseball
tagline: Nine innings, ninety feet, and failure three times in ten.
overview: Baseball is a bat-and-ball game in which one team pitches and fields while the other bats and runs the bases counterclockwise — first, second, third, home — to score runs. At its center is the duel of pitcher against batter, decided in under half a second. A regulation game is nine innings, and it simply does not end until someone leads after the last one.

It is America's summer ledger and East Asia's obsession: Japan's Koshien tournament fills a 47,000-seat stadium with teenagers, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela mint superstars from sandlots, and the World Baseball Classic has grown into a genuinely global championship. Nowhere else does a season stitch itself into nightly ritual quite like this — 162 games, radio on the porch, October at stake.

The newcomer's first lesson is geometric: the diamond is 90 feet (27.4 m) between bases, and almost every play is decided by half-steps. The second is statistical: even the greatest hitters fail seven times in ten — make peace with that early. Learn to read the count, and every pitch becomes a miniature drama.
facts: 1845 — the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club's rules; the first recorded match followed in June 1846 at Hoboken, New Jersey
World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC, formed 2013 by merger); Major League Baseball runs the top professional leagues
9 fielders (10 with the designated hitter); MLB active rosters of 26
Nine innings — about two hours 45 at the MLB level since the 2023 pitch clock
A diamond with 90 ft (27.4 m) base paths; the pitcher's rubber 60 ft 6 in (18.44 m) from home; fences typically 325-410 ft
A medal sport 1992-2008 and 2020; on the program again for Los Angeles 2028
MLB's 30 clubs plus major professional leagues in Japan (NPB), South Korea (KBO), Mexico, and Taiwan
history: Town-ball variants evolve into codified 'base ball'; the Knickerbocker Club writes the rules that stick.
The Cincinnati Red Stockings become the first openly professional club; the National League is founded in 1876.
The American League (founded 1901) and National League champions meet in the first modern World Series — Boston over Pittsburgh.
Babe Ruth turns the home run into the sport's currency and lifts it past the 1919 Black Sox scandal.
Jackie Robinson debuts for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, breaking MLB's color line — the most consequential day in the sport's history.
Baseball becomes an Olympic medal sport and launches the World Baseball Classic (2006) as a true world championship.
Shohei Ohtani becomes the first two-way star in a century, a pitch clock arrives in MLB (2023), and the game gets crisper.
formats: Nine-inning pro game
The MLB, NPB, and international standard: nine innings, extra innings until decided, and the designated hitter.
Professional leagues worldwide
Japan's NPB (12 clubs) and Korea's KBO run leagues with their own rules, rhythms, and devoted fan cultures.
World Baseball Classic
The national-team world championship, held since 2006 — the sport's true global title.
College baseball
Aluminum-bat NCAA format capped by the College World Series in Omaha each June.
Youth and amateur
Little League (founded 1939, its World Series in Williamsport since 1947), plus adult amateur and wood-bat summer leagues.
skills: Hitting
A rotational swing — load, stride, hips fire, hands inside the ball — timed against a ball that arrives in half a second.
Tee work and soft toss daily (50 swings), then batting-practice rounds; count hard contact per 15 swings, not home runs.
Fastball command
The four-seam fastball at the top of the zone; every other pitch works off it.
Bullpens to a four-quadrant target: 30 pitches a session, goal of 60 percent within a glove's width of the call.
Off-speed pitches
Changeup, slider, curveball — each moving off the fastball's plane and speed.
Learn the changeup first (grip change only, same arm speed): 20 throws a session before any spinning pitch; youth arms should wait on breaking balls.
Infield play
Pre-pitch ready position, funneling grounders with soft hands, footwork into a strong throw.
Ground-ball ladders of 50 at increasing pace, forehand and backhand; double-play turns with a sub-one-second release target.
Outfield play
Drop step, sprint to the catch point, receive over the throwing shoulder, crow hop to throw.
30 fungo flies read off the bat every session, plus crow-hop throws to a base on the run.
Catching (the position)
Receive quietly, frame the zone's edges, block balls in the dirt, and throw with intent.
Full-gear blocking drills — 30 dirt balls each direction — and pop-time throws to second under 2.0 seconds.
Baserunning
Sprint through first on grounders, round the bag on hits, read outfielders' arms for the extra base.
Time home-to-first weekly; drill leads, first-move reads, and tag-ups at every practice.
rules: Three outs end a half-inning; nine innings decide a game, and the home team bats last with the chance to walk it off.
The count: three strikes and you are out, four balls and you walk; a foul ball counts as a strike except with two strikes.
The strike zone spans home plate between the batter's knees and the midpoint of the torso, judged by the umpire or the electronic zone in some leagues.
Batters are out on strikes, on caught flies (runners must tag up), and on force or tag plays; runners must touch every base in order.
Scoring: one run per runner crossing home; a fair ball over the fence is a home run, and a grand slam with the bases loaded scores four.
Pitchers work from the stretch with runners on, and a balk — deceiving the runner — awards the next base.
MLB pace rules since 2023: a pitch clock of about 15 seconds with the bases empty and 18 with runners, plus limits on step-offs and mound visits.
equipment: Bat
Alloy or composite for amateurs, wood in the pros; a durable alloy bat runs $50-200.
Ball
Cork-centered, yarn-wrapped, leather-covered: 22.9-23.5 cm around and 142-149 g.
Glove
Leather and sized by position — 11-12 in for infielders, 12-13 for outfielders; $40-150 for a gamer.
Batting helmet
Mandatory at every level, $40-80, with an added face guard for juniors.
Catcher's gear
Mask-and-helmet, chest protector, shin guards, and a cup — the full kit runs $150-400 and is non-negotiable.
Cleats
Metal for pro and high-school varsity ball in the US, molded rubber for youth; $50-130.
training: Follow arm-care protocols: long-toss progressions, band work daily, and strict pitch counts with mandated rest — youth limits are law in the US.
Track hitting quality, not volume: exit velocity and hard-contact rate tell more than batting-practice home runs.
Train position-specific speed — catchers pop times, infielders first-step quickness (5-10-5 pro agility), outfielders straight-line sprints.
Batting and throwing both run on hip rotation: deadlifts, rotational med-ball throws, and oblique work twice a week.
Take ground balls and fungo flies daily; fielding reps decay faster than any other skill in the game.
pathway: Grassroots
Tee-ball at 4-6, then coach-pitch and kid-pitch Little League — the sport's front door worldwide.
Youth travel and high school
Travel ball from around 10, school baseball, and the showcase-camp circuit in the early teens.
College or academy
NCAA and junior-college baseball, or MLB's international academies in the Dominican Republic and Venezuela.
Professional
The MLB draft (20 rounds each July) out of high school or college, then minor-league rungs from rookie ball to Triple-A; NPB and KBO routes abroad.
National team
World Baseball Classic and WBSC Premier12 selection at the top of the international ladder.
events: World Series
Best-of-seven each October between the AL and NL champions — baseball's championship since 1903.
World Baseball Classic
The national-team world championship, roughly every three years since 2006; Japan has won three of the first five editions.
Japan Series
NPB's championship each October since 1950 — the climax of Japan's baseball year.
College World Series
Every June in Omaha, Nebraska — eight teams, bracket madness in the summer sun.
Little League World Series
Every August in Williamsport, Pennsylvania since 1947 — 10-to-12-year-olds on national television.
legends: Babe Ruth
New York Yankees — 714 home runs and a .690 career slugging percentage untouched a century later; the man who invented the long ball.
Willie Mays
New York and San Francisco — 660 home runs, 12 Gold Gloves, and 'The Catch' in the 1954 World Series.
Satchel Paige
Negro Leagues immortal who finally reached MLB at 42 — 'Don't look back, something might be gaining on you.'
Shohei Ohtani
Los Angeles — the first true two-way star since Ruth; 2024 brought the first 50-homer, 50-steal season in MLB history.
Ichiro Suzuki
Japan's hit machine — 3,000-plus MLB hits after 1,278 in NPB, elected to the Hall of Fame in 2025.
getting_started: Get a glove first and break it in properly — play catch 15 minutes daily for two weeks before anything else.
Learn to hit off a tee; the tee is not for children, it is where big leaguers take their daily swings.
Find a rec league, beer league, or pickup game — adult baseball and its softball cousins exist nearly everywhere.
Play catch with a purpose: pick a target on your partner's body and hit it 50 times without a wild throw.
Watch one game a week with the count in mind — guess fastball or breaking ball before every pitch.
Learn to score a game by hand; nine innings of scorekeeping teaches the rules faster than a rulebook.
glossary: Strike zone
The invisible box over the plate between the knees and mid-torso where strikes live.
Full count
Three balls, two strikes — the pitch everyone leans forward for.
Double play
Two outs on one batted ball, usually shortstop to second to first — 'around the horn.'
Southpaw
A left-handed pitcher, from the era when ballparks faced east and the arm faced south.
Can of corn
An easy fly ball — taken, like everything else, off the grocer's top shelf.
Grand slam
A home run with the bases loaded: four runs, one swing.
Balk
An illegal deception of runners by the pitcher — a free base and a chorus of boos.
Foul tip
A sharply struck ball glancing off the bat into the catcher's glove — a strike, and live with two strikes.
Closer
The relief pitcher brought in for the final outs — entrance music mandatory.
Bush league
Slang for unsporting or amateurish play — an insult older than the designated hitter.

name: Softball (Fastpitch and Slowpitch)
tagline: Baseball's windmill cousin — 43 feet of pure reaction, seven quick innings.
overview: Softball is baseball's closest relative, played on a smaller diamond with a bigger yellow ball pitched underhand. In fastpitch — the international and collegiate format — the pitcher whips a full windmill delivery from 43 feet, generating rise balls and drops that reach the plate in less time than an MLB fastball. Seven innings decide it; the geometry is tighter, and everything happens faster.

Invented indoors at a Chicago boat club in 1887 as a winter baseball substitute, softball grew into one of the most-played team sports in the United States and a women's collegiate giant — the Women's College World Series sells out Oklahoma City every June. Slowpitch recreation leagues, with their arcing pitches and post-game traditions, may be the most sociable team sport ever devised.

Newcomers should know fastpitch is a pitcher's game first: a dominant one can carry a team through a tournament, and every roster decision flows from who is in the circle. Batters work with tiny margins, so slapping and bunting are weapons, not clichés. And the defense plays shallow, because at 60 feet everything arrives early.
facts: 1887 — the first game is played indoors at Chicago's Farragut Boat Club; the name 'softball' takes hold by the mid-1920s
World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC), formed 2013 by merging baseball's and softball's international federations
9 fielders a side (10 with the extra fielder in some slowpitch codes)
Seven innings — college and international games usually finish inside two hours
60 ft (18.29 m) base paths; the pitcher's plate 43 ft (13.11 m) from home in women's fastpitch; fences about 200-220 ft
Optic yellow, 12 in (30.5 cm) around and 178-198 g — bigger and heavier than a baseball
Women's fastpitch 1996-2008 and 2020; on the program again for Los Angeles 2028
1965 — the first women's world championship in Melbourne; the men's followed in 1966
history: Awaiting a football score at the Farragut Boat Club, alumni improvise a game with a tied-up boxing glove and a broom handle; George Hancock writes the first rules.
The name 'softball' sticks at a national tournament run alongside Chicago's World's Fair — the sport's coming-out party.
The International Softball Federation forms (1952); the first women's world championship is held in Melbourne (1965).
Women's fastpitch is added to the Olympics and debuts at Atlanta 1996 — the USA wins gold, and again in 2000 and 2004.
Voted off the Olympic program after Beijing 2008, softball returns at Tokyo 2020, where Japan beats the USA for gold again.
Athletes Unlimited launches its points-based pro league (2020) and softball regains its Olympic slot for Los Angeles 2028.
formats: Fastpitch
The Olympic and collegiate format: windmill pitching at 70 mph from 43 feet, bunting and slapping, seven innings.
Slowpitch
The recreational giant — the pitch must arc 6-12 feet, a tenth fielder is common, and home runs are often capped per team.
College (NCAA)
Seven innings with the designated player, run-rule mercy, and a postseason that ends in Oklahoma City.
Modified pitch
The middle path — underhand but no windmill; common in adult recreational leagues.
Coed and corporate leagues
Slowpitch's social engine: batting orders that alternate men and women, and games that end wherever the evening goes.
skills: Windmill pitching
A full-circle arm whip generating speed and spin — legal underhand, and from 43 feet, devastatingly quick.
Bullpens of 60-100 pitches daily: 20 fastballs at a spot, then spins — track called-strike percentage, not velocity alone.
Rise ball
A pitch thrown with backward spin that appears to hop as it reaches the plate — fastpitch's signature weapon.
Isolate the grip and snap with 25 half-speed reps, then full speed; the goal is late lift at the top of the zone.
Changeup
The equalizer: identical arm speed, a ball that arrives a beat late.
Pair it with every fastball session — 10 changeups per 60 pitches — and chase a 10-mph gap off the fastball.
Slap hitting
Left-side batters running through the box while making contact, beating the ball to first with pure speed.
Dry footwork 30 times without a ball, then soft toss; the standard is ball down and out of the box within three seconds to first.
Bunting
Deadening the ball on purpose — sacrifice, squeeze, and slap-bunt variants that move runners 60 feet at a time.
25 bunts a session to chalked zones down each line; five of six in fair territory before squeeze practice begins.
Infield quickness
At 60 feet the game is anticipation: glove readiness and transfer speed rule the infield.
Reaction-ball work plus 50 ground balls a day at game speed, fielding and releasing in under a second.
Throwing mechanics
Overhand throwing with a crow hop from the outfield and quick snaps infield — arm strength is trained, not inherited.
Long toss three times a week out to 120 feet with daily band work; 20 on-target throws to bases each session.
rules: Seven innings; the visiting team bats first, and the home team walks it off if ahead after batting in the seventh.
Fastpitch: an underhand windmill delivery from 43 feet, with runners released from their bases only once the ball leaves the pitcher's hand.
Slowpitch: the pitch must arc between 6 and 12 feet, and home runs past a league's cap are ruled dead-ball outs.
The look-back rule: with the pitcher holding the ball inside the 8-foot circle, runners must immediately advance or return — no dancing off base.
Balls, strikes, force outs, and tag-ups mirror baseball, but the 60-foot diamond and big ball make the short game king.
Most codes end a game early when a team leads by 8 or more runs after five innings.
Late extra innings use the international tiebreaker — each half-inning begins with a runner on second base.
equipment: Ball
Optic yellow, 12 in around and 178-198 g; the 16-inch 'Chicago' ball is famously played barehanded.
Bat
Composite or alloy, no more than 34 in long and 2.25 in in diameter; competitive fastpitch bats run $80-300.
Glove
Leather, 11.5-13 in, plus a first-base mitt and a catcher's mitt as in baseball; $50-200.
Cleats
Molded for youth, metal permitted at college and international level; $50-130.
Fielder's mask
A protective face mask for the circle and the corner infield positions — increasingly standard, $40-70.
Batting helmet
With an attached facemask, mandatory at nearly every level of fastpitch; $50-100.
training: Pitchers are volume athletes: daily band work, heavy leg and hip strength (the windmill runs on the legs), and pitch counts with mandated rest.
Hitters train against elite velocity with short toss from 25 feet — compress reaction time on purpose, twice a week.
Slappers live on footwork: home-to-first under 2.9 seconds is the standard worth chasing.
Defense plays shallow and fast — reaction-ball circuits and 5-10-5 agility twice weekly.
Catchers chase sub-1.9-second pop times to second: blocking drills and footwork every session, throwing every other.
pathway: Grassroots
Recreation leagues and coach-pitch juniors — most players start at 7 or 8, often on the same diamonds as their parents.
Travel ball (10U-18U)
The club showcase circuit: tournaments most weekends from age 10, college coaches watching at 16U and 18U.
High school and college
Varsity seasons plus NCAA, NAIA, or junior-college ball — Division I alone has nearly 300 programs.
Professional
Athletes Unlimited in the US and Japan's JD.League, arguably the deepest pitching pool on earth.
National team
WBSC World Cups and Olympic selection — the USA and Japan are the sport's two superpowers.
events: Women's College World Series
Every June in Oklahoma City — the pinnacle of the collegiate game since 1982, played to a packed house.
WBSC Women's Softball World Cup
Every two years since 1965 — the USA leads the all-time medal table, with Japan owning much of the recent era.
Olympic softball
Women's fastpitch 1996-2008 and 2020; back on the program for Los Angeles 2028.
Athletes Unlimited
A US professional league since 2020 with individual-points scoring and rotating captain-drafted teams.
JD.League
Japan's professional league since 2022, successor to the Japan Softball League — where the world's best pitchers work.
legends: Jennie Finch
USA — Athens 2004 gold and Beijing 2008 silver; a 6-ft-1 right-hander whose rise ball made her the sport's most famous face.
Lisa Fernandez
USA — three Olympic golds (1996, 2000, 2004) as a dominant pitcher and hitter; perhaps the greatest all-round fastpitch player.
Cat Osterman
USA — left-handed ace with 2004 gold and two silvers, plus 2,265 strikeouts at Texas in one of the most dominant NCAA careers ever.
Dot Richardson
USA — hit the first home run in Olympic softball history in the 1996 gold-medal game; two Olympic golds.
Monica Abbott
USA — 2,440 strikeouts at Tennessee, still the NCAA Division I record, and a globe-trotting professional icon.
getting_started: Find a glove and a league first: adult slowpitch needs no more than that, and registration is usually open all summer.
If fastpitch calls, find a pitching coach early — the windmill is too technical to self-teach safely.
Practice the underhand arc with a bucket of balls and a strike zone drawn on a wall; slowpitch accuracy is a quickly earned skill.
Learn slap footwork left-handed even if you hit right-handed — the skill adds a roster spot's worth of value.
Play catch two or three times a week and take 50 dry swings; softball hands reward cheap, frequent reps.
Watch one Women's College World Series game — the pace and the crowds will recalibrate what you think the sport is.
glossary: Windmill
The legal fastpitch delivery: one full arm circle, with the hips and legs doing the firing.
Rise ball
A backspinned pitch that appears to hop at the plate.
Drop ball
The opposite: a pitch that falls off the table at the front knee.
Slapper
A left-handed batter who runs through the box while contacting the ball.
Circle
The 8-foot radius around the pitcher's plate that triggers the look-back rule.
International tiebreaker
The extra-inning format starting each half-inning with a runner on second.
Crow hop
The outfielder's hop-step that turns a catch into a throw.
Frozen rope
A line drive hit flat and hard, on a string.
Full count
Three balls, two strikes — everyone in the park leans in.
Play at the plate
The throw home against a charging runner — fastpitch's signature collision of timing.

name: Rugby Union
tagline: Fifteen a side, eighty minutes, and every tackle a contest for the ball.
overview: Rugby union is a full-contact game of 15 a side — eight forwards and seven backs — in which the ball may only be passed backwards and ground is gained by running, kicking, and contesting every tackle. Score by grounding the ball over the try line for five points, or add conversions, penalties, and drop goals. Two 40-minute halves, and the clock almost never stops.

Born at Rugby School — legend says William Webb Ellis picked up the ball and ran in 1823 — and codified in 1871, the game became the civic religion of New Zealand, where the All Blacks' haka opens every Test, and much of the British Isles, France, South Africa, and the Pacific. The 1995 World Cup final, with Nelson Mandela in a Springbok jersey handing the trophy to Francois Pienaar, remains one of sport's great political images.

Newcomers should learn two things early: the tackle is a contest for the ball, not the end of the play — players arrive and fight for possession on the ground — and everyone on the field runs, passes, tackles, and occasionally kicks. The game looks chaotic at first; watch the tackled ball rather than the ball carrier, and the chaos resolves into law.
facts: 1871 — the Rugby Football Union forms in London; the first international, Scotland v England, follows that year in Edinburgh
World Rugby — founded 1886 as the International Rugby Football Board, with more than 100 member unions
15 a side (8 forwards, 7 backs) plus up to 8 replacements; match-day squads of 23
A pitch no larger than 100 x 70 m plus in-goal areas; goalposts 5.6 m apart with the crossbar at 3 m
Try 5 points, conversion 2, penalty goal 3, drop goal 3
Fifteens appeared 1900-1924; rugby sevens returned the sport to the Games at Rio 2016
1987 — New Zealand wins the inaugural tournament, co-hosted with Australia
history: The legend: William Webb Ellis, 'with a fine disregard for the rules of football,' takes the ball in his arms and runs at Rugby School — the trophy still bears his name.
Twenty-one clubs form the RFU; Scotland beats England in the first international at Raeburn Place, Edinburgh.
The IRFB forms to write the laws (1886); in 1895 the split over broken-time payments creates the Northern Union — rugby league, with a page of its own.
The Original All Blacks tour Britain and popularize running rugby; union appears in four Olympics (1900-1924) before leaving the Games.
The first Rugby World Cup — 16 teams, won by New Zealand — takes the sport global on television.
The World Cup in South Africa: the game declares itself open to professionals, and Mandela hands Pienaar the trophy in a rainbow jersey.
Rugby sevens debuts at the Rio Olympics — Fiji wins the men's gold, its first Olympic medal of any kind.
formats: Fifteens (XV)
The full game: 15 a side with scrums, lineouts, and mauls — the format of Test rugby and the World Cup.
Rugby sevens
7 a side, 7-minute halves, a whole tournament in a weekend — the Olympic and World Series format.
Tens
A one-day hybrid: 10 a side, 10-minute halves, kept alive by famous invitation tournaments.
Women's fifteens and sevens
A professional era of its own — the Women's Rugby World Cup since 1991, Olympic sevens since 2016, and contracted leagues in England and France.
Club and social rugby
Saturday club rugby in a hundred countries — where most of the world's rugby is actually played.
Vets and golden oldies
Over-35s rugby under modified laws — proof the sport can be played, gingerly, for life.
skills: Passing
Delivering the ball backwards off both hands — long, flat, and fast across the body.
Passing under fatigue: 3 x 2 minutes of shuttle passing with a partner; accuracy gate of 8 of 10 through a 1 m target at 10 m.
Tackling
Shoulder-led contact with the head on the safe side and the legs driving — then an immediate fight for the ball.
Progress from bags to live 1 v 1: 40 technique reps weekly; the law demands you release the tackled player and roll away.
Breakdown (ruck) work
The fight over the tackled ball: arriving low, on your feet, clearing past the ball.
Sled and shield circuits of 6 x 20 seconds with a coach calling arrival or cleanout; height wins turnovers.
Scrummaging
Eight forwards bound and pushing in sync — a coordinated power contest for the feed.
Scrum-machine sessions of 5 x 30-second drives, technique before weight, plus mandatory weekly neck and shoulder strength.
Lineout throwing and lifting
The hooker's throw to a lifted jumper — a basketball play with two props as elevators.
30 throws a session to three marked targets; jumpers and lifters drill timing with the same pod every week.
Evasive running
Sidestep, swerve, and the fend — beating a defender one-on-one in a foot of space.
1 v 1 into a 5 m channel, 10 lives per player; track beaten defenders, not just tries.
Place kicking
The match-winning skill: striking off the tee over the crossbar from any angle.
30 kicks a session — 10 each from in front, the 22, and wide; log percentage from each zone and chase the weak ones.
rules: The ball may not be passed forward — it travels backward from hand to hand while play runs continuously.
The tackled player must release the ball immediately and roll away; arriving players must stay on their feet to contest it — that contest is the ruck.
A try — grounding the ball in-goal — is worth 5 points; conversions 2; penalty and drop goals 3.
Offside is everywhere: players must stay behind the hindmost foot of the ruck and behind the kicker's last foot at kicks.
Scrums restart play after minor infringements — eight forwards per side bind and push, and the hooker strikes for the ball.
Lineouts restart play when the ball goes into touch: jumpers are lifted to contest the throw-in.
A yellow card means 10 minutes in the sin bin; a red card means off for good.
equipment: Ball
An oval size-5 match ball (smaller sizes for juniors); $50-120 buys a ball that lasts seasons.
Mouthguard
Mandatory at every serious level — $10 boil-and-bite to $200 custom dental fittings.
Headgear and shoulder pads
Thin, World Rugby-approved padding — comfort rather than armor; $30-80 for either.
Boots
Studs for grip with toe reinforcement for kicking; $60-150.
Kit
Jersey, shorts, and socks built to be grabbed — reinforced seams are worth the money.
Training gear
Hit shields, tackle bags, and a breakdown sled are the furniture of every club; the club buys, you show up.
training: Match demands are brutal: backs cover 6-8 km with repeated collisions — build an aerobic base, then repeated-sprint intervals such as 6 x 50 m shuttles.
Collision conditioning before collisions: neck flexion and trap-bar deadlifts gate every contact block.
Hamstrings and adductors are rugby's soft-tissue tax — Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks twice weekly.
Arriving at the breakdown on your feet is a trained skill: sled drives beat gym machines for it.
Play sevens in summer and fifteens in winter — the formats feed each other skills and set-piece.
pathway: Grassroots
Club minis from age 5-6 and school rugby — the sport's true base in every playing nation.
School and age-grade
Representative school and age-grade rugby; in New Zealand and South Africa, school 1st XV matches are televised.
Academy and provincial
Franchise and provincial academies at 16-18 — contracted development squads below the professional first XV.
Professional
The Premiership (England), Top 14 (France), United Rugby Championship, Super Rugby, and Japan's League One pay the bills.
International
Test rugby — the Six Nations, the Rugby Championship, and the World Cup every four years.
events: Rugby World Cup
Every four years since 1987, now with 20 teams — the Webb Ellis Cup is the sport's biggest prize.
Six Nations
Every February-March — England, France, Ireland, Italy, Scotland, and Wales in the northern hemisphere's annual championship.
The Rugby Championship
Annually — Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa in the southern hemisphere's Test series.
British & Irish Lions tour
Every four years — the best of Britain and Ireland tours South Africa, Australia, or New Zealand.
World Rugby SVNS Series
The annual global sevens circuit for men and women, from Dubai to Hong Kong, with Olympic qualification attached.
legends: Jonah Lomu
New Zealand — a 1.96 m, 119 kg winger who ran over England in the 1995 World Cup semifinal; the professional era's first global superstar.
Richie McCaw
New Zealand — 148 Tests, the most-capped All Black, and captain of back-to-back World Cup wins in 2011 and 2015.
Dan Carter
New Zealand — fly-half with a record 1,598 Test points, three World Player of the Year awards, and the 2015 final's man-of-the-match.
Siya Kolisi
South Africa — the Springboks' first Black captain, who lifted the Webb Ellis Cup in 2019 and again in 2023.
Portia Woodman
New Zealand — Black Ferns wing; 2017 World Cup winner and top try-scorer at that tournament, plus Olympic sevens gold at Tokyo.
getting_started: Find your local club — rugby clubs recruit beginners at every age and own the social calendar of most towns that have them.
Learn to fall first: breakfalls and tackle technique before contact, always under supervision.
Pass every day against a wall or with a partner — 100 backward passes, both hands, both sides.
Get fit for the game, not the mirror: shuttles, sleds, and bodyweight circuits beat mirror muscles.
Watch one full Test match with the breakdown in view — count the turnovers, not the tries.
Buy the mouthguard before the boots; the rest of the kit can wait a month.
glossary: Try
A score, worth 5 — named for the original reward, a 'try' at goal.
Ruck
The contest for the ball on the ground after a tackle.
Maul
The ball carrier held up, teammates bound on, all moving forward — a rolling argument.
Grubber
A low bouncing kick along the ground, chased by everyone.
Garryowen
The up-and-under — a high kick to contest; named for the Irish club.
Dummy pass
Faking the pass to fix a defender, then going yourself.
Sin bin
Where yellow-carded players sit for 10 minutes while their team fights on short-handed.
Advantage
The referee playing on after an infringement because the offended team is gaining ground.
Grand Slam
A Six Nations title won with victories over all five rivals.
Haka
The All Blacks' pre-match challenge — the most famous 80 seconds in sport.

name: Rugby League
tagline: Born of the 1895 split: thirteen players, six tackles, relentless speed.
overview: Rugby league is rugby's working-class offshoot: 13 a side, and when a player is tackled the ball is heeled back in a play-the-ball and the game restarts instantly. The attacking team gets six tackles to advance before possession turns over, which is why the fifth tackle usually ends in a kick. It is rugby stripped for speed — fewer stoppages, more running, and collisions on every carry.

The 1895 meeting at Huddersfield's George Hotel — northern English clubs breaking from the RFU over payments to working men — created a sport that became the heartbeat of northern England, of New South Wales and Queensland, and of Papua New Guinea, where it is the national game. State of Origin, the annual interstate war between New South Wales and Queensland, is Australian sport at its most ferocious.

Newcomers should count with the game: six tackles to a set, and the scoreboard follows the sets. Watch how the ball moves — a dummy-half dart here, two passes wide there, a bomb launched on the last. Learn the play-the-ball, the game's metronome, and the tempo makes sense.
facts: 1895 — 22 northern English clubs form the Northern Union at the George Hotel, Huddersfield, over broken-time payments
International Rugby League for the world game; the Rugby Football League (England) and the Australian Rugby League Commission run the top competitions
13 a side; NRL match-day squads of 17 (four on the bench) with eight interchanges
Two 40-minute halves, with the clock stopped for tries and conversions in the NRL
The same maximum as union — 100 x 68 m plus in-goals; posts 5.6 m apart
Try 4 points, conversion 2, penalty goal 2, drop goal 1
1954 — rugby league's World Cup predates union's by 33 years; Great Britain won the first
Northern England, New South Wales and Queensland, Papua New Guinea (the national sport), plus France, New Zealand, and the Pacific islands
history: The Great Split: clubs meet at the George Hotel and form the Northern Union — professionalism for working-class players is the issue.
The Northern Union cuts teams to 13 a side and replaces the post-tackle scrum with the play-the-ball — rugby league becomes its own sport.
New Zealand's 'All Golds' take the professional game to Britain and on to Australia; leagues start in Sydney in 1908 — the sport's Pacific future begins.
The first Rugby League World Cup — the oldest rugby World Cup — is won by Great Britain.
State of Origin begins, with players representing their state of origin: it becomes Australian sport's fiercest annual rivalry.
The Super League war between News Corporation and the ARL splits the game, then reshapes it; the NRL is born from the peace in 1998.
The World Cup grows into a men's, women's, and wheelchair festival (the 2021 edition played in 2022) — Australia has won 12 of the 16 men's titles.
formats: Thirteens (the international game)
13 a side, six tackles, 80 minutes — the format of the NRL, Super League, and internationals.
Nines
9 a side, 9-minute halves, whole tournaments in a day — the festival format that fills pre-season weekends.
Women's rugby league
The NRLW (since 2018), women's State of Origin, and a Women's Rugby League World Cup running since 2000.
Masters (over-35s)
Modified contact laws for older players — two tags per tackle and no lifting.
Schoolboy and junior league
The nursery: schoolboy competitions in Sydney and Leeds have fed both hemispheres for a century.
skills: Play-the-ball speed
Getting to your feet and heeling the ball back instantly — the game's metronome.
Hit-and-roll drills: 3 x 10 quick play-the-balls against shields, chasing a sub-two-second turnaround from tackle to dummy-half pass.
Dummy-half running
The hooker sniping around the ruck before the defense resets — noting that being touched in possession turns the ball over.
Scoot drills: 10 per session against a retreating line; only count the ones that gain five meters or force a defensive shift.
The bomb
A towering kick into the in-goal for chasing wingers to contest in the air.
20 bombs a session with hang time measured by a partner; wingers contest each one with a catcher under it.
Offload
Passing in the tackle — second-phase play that turns set defenses into chaos.
Bag offloads: 20 reps with a support player calling; the ball must go backwards or it is a penalty.
Hit-and-spin
Taking the collision on your terms — shoulder in, spin out of the tackle, ball alive.
1 v 2 collisions and wrestle circuits 20 minutes twice a week; league's ruck is a wrestling gym.
Line defense
A defensive line that moves as one, three or four men to a shoulder, with no gaps.
Line-speed sets of 6 x 10 — all 13 sliding together; integrity of the line beats individual heroics.
Short kicking
Grubbers, cross-field chips, and field goals — turning tackles into points with the last touch of the set.
Kicking sessions of 40 balls: grubbers into the in-goal, chips to the corner, plus 20 shots at goal.
rules: Thirteen players a side; possession turns over at the completion of the sixth tackle if no score has come.
The tackled player stands and heels the ball back in the play-the-ball; two markers may defend directly, and the rest of the line retreats 10 m.
Scoring: try 4, conversion 2, penalty goal 2, drop goal 1 — the single point has decided a hundred famous matches.
The 40/20 rule: a kick from inside your own 40 that bounces into touch inside the opponent's 20 earns the kicking team a scrum feed and fresh set.
Forward passes and knock-ons are penalized with scrums, now largely uncontested restarts that keep the clock honest.
A yellow card means 10 minutes in the sin bin; shoulder charges and contact with the head draw severe sanctions.
Interchanges are capped — eight per match in the NRL — so forwards ration their tanks across 80 minutes.
equipment: Ball
The league ball is slightly smaller and more pointed than union's, built for passing and kicking; $50-100.
Boots
Light and low for speed, with screw-in studs for grass; $60-150.
Mouthguard
Mandatory at every level — the collisions are constant; $10-40.
Headgear and shoulder pads
Thin approved padding, common among outside backs and front-rowers alike; $30-80.
Training gear
Wrestle mats, tackle bags, and shields — the wrestling element makes mats a league-club staple.
Kit
Reinforced jerseys built for stretching, grabbing, and 30 tackles a match.
training: League may be the most aerobically punishing collision sport: backs cover 8-9 km — train repeat high-intensity efforts such as 6 x 40 m sprints off short recoveries.
The wrestle is a skill gym: clubs train jiu-jitsu-style grips and leg drives for the ruck, twice weekly.
Wingers hit 35 km/h and above — flywheel or resisted sprint work for the outside backs.
Neck, shoulder, and hamstring protocols are non-negotiable: Nordics, Copenhagen planks, and neck flexion in every week.
Bomb-squad practice under fatigue: high balls caught in the last five minutes decide close games, so train them tired.
pathway: Junior league (U6-U16)
Local clubs from age 6 — the lifeblood of the game in New South Wales and Queensland.
Representative pathways
Age-grade competitions run by NRL clubs — the Harold Matthews Cup (U16s) and SG Ball Cup (U18s) are the famous rungs.
Reserve grade and cup
The NSW Cup and Queensland Cup bridge young professionals into the top grade.
Professional
The NRL (17 clubs since 2023) and Super League in Europe — the two paying leagues at the center of the sport.
International
Kangaroos, Kiwis, England, and the Pacific nations, with a World Cup every four years.
events: NRL Grand Final
One Sunday each spring in Sydney — Australia's rugby league championship day.
State of Origin
Three matches every mid-season, New South Wales v Queensland — routinely among Australian television's biggest nights.
Super League Grand Final
Every October at Old Trafford — the climax of the northern English season since 1996.
Challenge Cup
A knockout cup since 1896 with a Wembley final tradition — every amateur club in the draw.
Rugby League World Cup
Every four years since 1954 — the oldest rugby World Cup, with men's, women's, and wheelchair editions running together.
legends: Clive Churchill
'The Little Master' — South Sydney and Australian fullback of the 1950s; the NRL grand final's man-of-the-match medal bears his name.
Wally Lewis
'The King' — Queensland and Australian five-eighth, State of Origin's founding colossus; the series' best-player medal is his.
Andrew Johns
Newcastle's Immortal halfback — the kicking and vision that set the template for every modern playmaker.
Jonathan Thurston
North Queensland — a record four Dally M Medals and the 2015 premiership sealed in golden point; the era's supreme big-moment player.
Cameron Smith
Melbourne — record NRL appearances (430) and a record 42 State of Origin matches; captain of everything he played for.
getting_started: Find a local club — league clubs run juniors from age 5 and senior grades for every body type.
Learn the wrestle safely: grappling and play-the-ball technique under a coach before full contact.
Practice kick-catching weekly — the bomb is coming whether you like it or not.
Do your cardio homework before the first trial: repeat shuttles, not long slow runs.
Watch one NRL match counting the sets — six tackles each, and note how rarely the ball is handled twice by the same player.
Pick your position honestly: the game has a place for the fast, the tall, and the immovable.
glossary: Play-the-ball
The heel-back restart after every tackle — league's signature.
Dummy half
The player scooting from behind the ruck, named for rugby's borrowed position.
Set of six
A team's six tackles — the currency of possession and field position.
Bomb
A towering kick into the in-goal, chased by leaping wingers.
Offload
A pass delivered in the tackle to keep the ball alive.
Markers
The two defenders standing over the play-the-ball.
A kick from inside your 40 into touch inside their 20 — a bonus set of six.
Second-phase play
Any play that continues after the tackle via an offload.
Field goal
The one-point drop kick, dropped from any distance and usually at a gallop — it wins tight finals.
Origin
State of Origin — Queensland v New South Wales, three nights a winter, no quarter asked.

name: American Football
tagline: Four downs, ten yards, eleven helmets — chess at a dead sprint.
overview: American football is 11-a-side territory warfare: the offense gets four downs — attempts — to advance the ball ten yards by running or passing; make it and the downs reset, fail and possession turns over. Scoring is a touchdown for 6, a field goal for 3, a safety for 2, with kicks and two-point tries after touchdowns. Every play begins from a snap and is a designed collision of 22 athletes.

No sport is more American or more strategic — NFL playbooks run hundreds of pages, and head coaches employ armies of coordinators. The Super Bowl is the most-watched television event in the United States every single year, college football fills 100,000-seat stadiums on Saturdays, and from Texas Friday nights to Ohio snow games, the sport is cultural bedrock.

Newcomers should watch the line of scrimmage before the snap: formations telegraph intent, and the quarterback's pre-snap reads are the opening moves. Second, live by the down counter and the yellow first-down line — they are your two best friends. The game rewards understanding more than almost any other; patient viewers become addicts within a season.
facts: November 6, 1869 — Rutgers beats Princeton 6-4 in the first intercollegiate contest, under soccer-derived rules
The NFL (founded 1920 as the APFA in Canton, Ohio); IFAF (1998) runs the international game
11 a side; NFL clubs carry 53-player rosters with roughly 48 active on game day
Four 15-minute quarters — stoppages stretch an NFL broadcast past three hours
100 yd x 53.3 yd (91.4 x 48.8 m) plus two 10-yd end zones; goalposts 18.5 ft wide above a 10-ft crossbar
Touchdown 6, extra point 1 or two-point try 2, field goal 3, safety 2
Not an Olympic medal sport — its flag football cousin debuts at Los Angeles 2028
history: Rutgers and Princeton play the first intercollegiate game; handling and the carried ball soon take over.
Walter Camp of Yale codifies the line of scrimmage, the down-and-distance system, and 11-man sides — the game's true father.
The American Professional Football Association forms in a Canton, Ohio car dealership with Jim Thorpe as its first president; it becomes the NFL in 1922.
The rival American Football League forces a merger; the first Super Bowl is played in January 1967 (Packers over Chiefs) and the modern NFL emerges in 1970.
The passing revolution: rules protecting quarterbacks and receivers turn the aerial game from gambit to gospel.
The league goes global — annual regular-season games abroad since 2007, a 17th game in 2021, and flag football joining the LA 2028 Olympics.
formats: NFL
32 clubs, 17-game regular seasons, and a 14-team playoff — the sport's pinnacle since 1920.
College football (NCAA)
The Saturday religion: the biggest stadiums in the sport and a 12-team playoff since the 2024-25 season.
Canadian football (CFL)
12 a side, three downs, and a longer, wider field — the Grey Cup has been contested since 1909.
Arena and indoor football
8 a side on a 50-yard field with rebound nets — the sport's arcade version.
Flag and touch football
The non-contact codes played by millions, and now the Olympic branch of the family.
skills: Quarterback passing
Throwing with anticipation — footwork, hip rotation, and a release that beats the receiver's break.
Daily drops (3- and 5-step) with 100 throws to targets at varied depths, then read progressions against air and defenders.
Route running
Selling every stem identically and breaking on a dime — separation is created at the top of the route.
Full-speed cone series through the route tree, 10 reps per cut; check the depth of every break on video.
Blocking
Hands inside, hips low, feet alive — the trade that wins no headlines and all games.
Sled and bag work of 3 x 10 drive blocks, plus 30-second mirror drills for pass sets.
Tackling
Shoulder-led with the head up — see what you hit; rugby-style tackling swept the sport for safety.
Form circuits without pads: fit position and tracking angles, 40 reps a week; never lead with the crown.
Catching
Plucking with the fingers away from the body, watching it in through contact.
100 catches a day off a machine or wall at varied angles, with low, high, and over-the-shoulder balls in every session.
Ball-carrier vision
One cut and go — reading the second level, juking or delivering the shoulder behind blocks.
Cone one-cut drills against a moving defender, 15 live reps a session; hesitation lives at the line, commitment past it.
Place kicking
Field goals and extra points — pure technique under maximum pressure.
20-30 kicks a session with grooved steps and consistent contact, logging makes by distance plus kickoff hang time.
rules: The offense has four downs to gain 10 yards; a first down resets the count, and failure on third down usually means a punt.
Scoring: touchdown 6, with an extra-point kick or a two-point try from the 2-yard line; field goal 3; safety 2.
The clock stops on incomplete passes and out-of-bounds plays, and each team gets three timeouts per half.
Seven players must line up on scrimmage, and only eligible receivers may touch a forward pass — the interior linemen do the hitting, not the catching.
Penalties cost 5, 10, or 15 yards — holding, pass interference, false starts — and the offended team may accept or decline.
Every scoring play and turnover is reviewed by replay, and coaches keep challenges for the rest.
Overtime: the NFL guarantees both teams a possession unless the first drive ends in a touchdown; playoff games never end in ties.
equipment: Helmet
A certified helmet ($150-400) with a position-specific facemask — the sport's most inspected piece of equipment.
Shoulder pads
Light shells for quarterbacks and receivers, armor for linemen; $100-300.
Cleats
Studs for grass, turf shoes for artificial surfaces; $60-150.
Football
The leather pro ball is about 28 cm long; youth and composite balls start at $20.
Integrated padding
Girdles with built-in hip, thigh, and knee pads, mandatory in most codes; $40-90.
Gloves
Sticky receiver gloves or padded lineman gloves; $30-80.
Mouthguard
Mandatory and cheap — $10-40, no exceptions at any sanctioned level.
training: Train alactic power: the average NFL play lasts about four seconds — 10-20 yard accelerations with full recovery, over and over.
The weight room is the sport's second field: trap-bar deadlifts for collision power, pressing and pulling for the constant hand-fighting.
Condition by position — linemen push sleds and wrestle; receivers and defensive backs run repeat 20-40 yard sprints with full rests.
Injury prevention centers on neck, knees, and concussions: neck-flexion protocols, landing mechanics, and modern tackling technique.
Film study is training: quarterbacks and safeties earn their living from the booth — a mental rep counts as a rep.
pathway: Youth leagues
Flag football first, then Pop Warner and local tackle leagues from around age 8-10.
High school
Friday night varsity football and the recruiting camp-and-combine circuit.
College
NCAA football with 85 scholarships per top-division program — the NFL's feeder system.
Professional
The NFL Draft each April, then training-camp cuts; the CFL and European leagues offer parallel roads.
International
IFAF world championships and fast-growing national programs from Germany to Japan's X-League.
events: Super Bowl
Every February since 1967 — the NFL's championship and the most-watched US broadcast of the year, every year.
NFL regular season and playoffs
32 teams, 17 games each since 2021, and a 14-team bracket through January.
College Football Playoff
The national championship, a 12-team bracket since the 2024-25 season, atop a bowl tradition a century old.
Grey Cup
Canada's championship, contested since 1909 under the CFL's three-down code.
NFL International Series
Regular-season games abroad every year since 2007 — London, Mexico City, Frankfurt — with new markets added.
legends: Jim Brown
Cleveland Browns (1957-65) — led the NFL in rushing in eight of nine seasons and never missed a game; the most dominant runner the sport has known.
Jerry Rice
San Francisco 49ers — 1,549 catches, 22,895 yards, and 197 receiving touchdowns, every major record, plus three Super Bowl rings.
Tom Brady
Seven Super Bowl titles — six with New England and one more in Tampa — plus the sport's career passing records; the greatest winner.
Walter Payton
Chicago Bears — 16,726 rushing yards stood as the record for two decades, and the NFL's man-of-the-year award still bears his nickname.
Lawrence Taylor
New York Giants — the outside linebacker rebuilt as a weapon: three Defensive Player of the Year awards and a title in 1986.
getting_started: Start with a football and a patch of grass: throw daily, and learn the spiral before any pad ever fits.
Play flag football to learn the positions and rules without the collisions.
Find a local amateur or semi-pro league — adult tackle football exists, insured and officiated, in most regions.
Watch one game a week with the down-and-distance in mind; predict run or pass before the snap.
Lift for power early — cleans, deadlifts, and sprints are the game's physical currency.
Learn one position deeply on film; football rewards the specialist's eye more than any sport.
glossary: Down
One play from scrimmage; four of them to make ten yards.
Snap
The exchange that starts every play — center to quarterback, at speed.
Blitz
Extra defenders rushing the passer, gambling on chaos.
Audible
A play changed at the line after the quarterback reads the defense.
Pick-six
An interception returned for a touchdown — the fastest swing in sport.
Red zone
Inside the opponent's 20-yard line, where the field shrinks and points are expected.
Hail Mary
A desperation deep pass into a crowd of receivers as time expires.
Pancake
A block that leaves the defender flat on the turf — an offensive lineman's trophy.
Sack
Tackling the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
Shotgun
The quarterback standing five yards deep to receive the snap, trading speed for protection.

name: Flag Football
tagline: American football minus the collisions: pull the flag, keep the speed.
overview: Flag football is American football without the collision: every player wears flags on a belt, and a ball carrier is stopped the instant an opponent pulls one away. Blocking is banned, everyone on offense is eligible to catch, and the game runs on speed and throwing. The standard international format is 5 v 5 on a short field — touchdown drives measured in seconds, not minutes.

Grown out of touch football on US military bases and recreation leagues, it is now among the fastest-growing sports on earth: millions of children in NFL FLAG leagues, national programs across dozens of countries, and an Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028 that lit the fuse on a professional era. Mexico and the United States contest the women's summit; the men's game runs deep across the Americas and Europe.

Newcomers will find the game friendlier than it looks — no padding needed, and the barrier to entry is a belt and a ball. But respect the skill: elite flag is chess at sprint speed, with quarterbacks reading defenses before the snap and releasing in under two seconds. Learn the no-run zones and the two-minute clock rules, and you are fluent.
facts: Played on US military bases in the 1940s; first national organizations in the 1960s, led by the National Touch Football League of St. Louis
IFAF (International Federation of American Football, founded 1998) runs the world game; NFL FLAG (launched 1996) runs the largest youth network
5 v 5 is the international standard, with squads of about 10
Two 20-minute halves with the clock stopped in the final two minutes of each
About 25 x 70 yards including two 10-yard end zones in NFL FLAG 5 v 5 — 50 yards of field between the goal lines
Debuts at the Los Angeles 2028 Games — men's and women's tournaments, approved by the IOC in October 2023
2002 — IFAF's first Flag Football World Championship in Austria (Austria men, Sweden women)
history: US military teams play touch-and-flag football through the war years — the collision-free version travels everywhere the service goes.
The National Touch Football League organizes in St. Louis; flag codes split from touch, the flag making every tackle objective.
The NFL launches NFL FLAG as a national youth program (1996); IFAF forms in 1998 to govern the international game.
IFAF stages the first Flag Football World Championship in Austria — the hosts win the men's title, Sweden the women's.
Flag football appears at the World Games in Birmingham, Alabama — Mexico's women beat the USA to gold behind quarterback Diana Flores.
The IOC approves flag football for Los Angeles 2028, and the NFL's Pro Bowl becomes a flag-format showcase in the same year.
formats: 5 v 5 (Olympic format)
The international standard: short field, four downs to midfield then four to score, with no-run zones near the markers.
NFL FLAG youth
Co-ed leagues for ages roughly 5-17 — the entry point for more than half a million children a year.
Adult recreational 4 v 4 and 8 v 8
Park, corporate, and social leagues with local house rules on rushing and running.
Women's elite
The women's game leads the sport's growth — Mexico v the USA is its clasico, with college and pro structures scaling up for 2028.
Elite national teams
IFAF world championships every two years, and Olympic tournaments from 2028 — the sport's summit.
skills: Flag pulling
The sport's tackle: track the carrier's hips, mirror, and scoop the flag cleanly off the belt in the open field.
1 v 1 pursuit drills — 10 live pulls a session at angles; close the gap in three seconds without losing contain.
Quick-release passing
Getting the ball out in under two seconds, because the rush arrives on a count.
Timed drop-backs with a stopwatch: drop, read one, then two, release — 50 reps against air or a coach's count.
Route running
Stems sold the same, breaks sharp and timed with the quarterback's drop — precision beats pure speed.
The full route tree against air, 10 reps each, then live versus press and off coverage.
Defensive mirroring
Backpedal, shadow the receiver's hips, and play the ball — with no contact allowed, feet are your hands.
30-second shadow technique rounds against a partner, then 1 v 1 reps where the win is a flag or an incompletion.
The snap
Every play starts with it: a crisp exchange — direct or shotgun — under pressure.
50 snaps a day to a target; the standard is zero bad exchanges per tournament.
Laterals and pitches
Backward pitches keep plays alive — flag's answer to the rugby offload, legal and lethal in the open field.
Two-on-one read drills: pitch or keep, 15 live reps a session with the lone defender deciding.
Reading zones
Quarterbacks identify zone or man before the snap; receivers find the soft spots and sit or split them.
Walk-through reads with the coverage called aloud pre-snap — 20 a practice — then verify each call with a partner scoring you.
rules: No contact: no blocking, tackling, or diving — the flag makes the tackle, and contact beyond the incidental is a penalty.
The ball is dead the moment a flag is pulled or the ball touches the ground — fumbles are dead balls, not scrambles.
Four downs to reach midfield for a first down, then four more to score; fail and the opponent takes over on offense.
In NFL FLAG rules the quarterback may not run the ball across the line of scrimmage — handoffs open the run game — and no-run zones sit five yards from midfield and the goal line.
Defenses may rush the passer on a set count, usually with one designated rusher, while the quarterback works against a pass clock.
Two 20-minute halves, with the clock stopped inside the final two minutes of each.
Touchdowns are worth 6 with 1- and 2-point conversions from set distances; safeties exist in most codes.
equipment: Flag belt
The sport's signature — the belt and its flags, $10-25; check your league's rules for two- or three-flag sets.
Football
Youth or intermediate size, smaller than the pro ball; $20-60.
Cleats
Turf or grass shoes — the sport's biggest performance purchase at $50-120.
Mouthguard
Recommended — collisions are accidental but real at pace; $10-30.
Receiver gloves
Grip gloves for cold or wet weather, $30-70.
Bibs and cones
Colored pinnies and a dozen cones turn any park into a field — under $30.
training: The game is repeat sprints: 10-15 plays per drive — train 20-40 yard bursts off short recoveries plus change-of-direction ladders twice weekly.
Quarterbacks build arm endurance with daily volume — 100-plus balls — because flag QBs throw more per minute than any code.
